# Who Jesus was for us

One command that ripped open every settled life among us: sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. Antony took it as though it had been said to him alone. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than anything else - an order to be obeyed, not a saying to be studied.

The Word who took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing our birth he might make us share what is his. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all.

The one whose cross changed what death could do. Death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. When persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer asked of us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. That continuity was not a substitute we invented. It was how we understood what his death had already won.

And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. We told that enemy to its own face: your coming has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you.

We never spoke of the healings among us as ours. One of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man: we are not the doers of these things. It is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe in him.

That is who he was to us: the one who gave the order we obeyed, who shared our birth so we could share his nature, who stripped death of its power, and who still worked through us when we did what we could not do alone.

We had the same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it.

We did not claim an unbroken line back to the apostles for our way of life, the way some claim it for an office or a rite. What we can honestly say is that no one man invented it whole. Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. Our founder sought him out and copied him before going further alone. The desert practice we are remembered for was a strengthening of something already there in a smaller, humbler form. It was not a new thing appearing out of nowhere.

The path was this: Scripture, read in the church's own gathering, heard as a direct command. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a saying to be studied - an order to be obeyed. That is how the connection ran for us - not through an argued chain of custody, but through words we took as living address.

You are asking about a struggle we did not write down in the form you are hoping for. We have no account from among us of someone who doubted and then came to believe - the kind of story where a person crosses from one side to the other and the crossing itself is what gets told [[desert.limit.doubt-and-doctrine]].

What we have instead is something smaller and less satisfying, maybe, but honest. We remember a man named Moses who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer before he came to us - a man other people were afraid of. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. The struggle stayed visible in what we kept about him. It was not smoothed away into an instant change. And Antony went into church one day not long after he lost his parents and heard the Gospel being read - the Lord telling the rich young man, if you would be perfect, go and sell what you have, give to the poor, and come follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. He walked out of the church, and before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Not long after, he heard the same Gospel read again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and he gave away the rest as well. He placed his sister with women he trusted, women already given to a life of virginity. Then he began the discipline himself, close to home at first, seeking out and copying an old man who was already living that way nearby. Even his own giving, in other words, took him two hearings to complete, not one decisive act.

We cannot promise you a sudden certainty. Nothing in what we kept suggests one was promised to us either. What we can tell you plainly is that staying in the struggle, without forcing a feeling you do not have, was itself how belief was held among us. The fight finding you is not your failure. You decide whether it moves in.

We held plainly, once we were called to say so, that the Son of God is not some lesser, created thing, not brought into being out of nothing, but the Eternal Word of the Father's own being. There was never a time when he was not. That was the faith we were formed in, and we refused communion with anyone who taught otherwise.

The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason one of us gave for why he came at all - not to save us by staying distant, but by becoming what we are so we could become what he is.

About the Spirit's own relation to the Father and the Son - whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or through the Son, whether the three are named in strict order or understood together - we did not argue that out in the form your question asks. Most of us were not formed to argue doctrine for a living. We were formed to see him. What we held we held mostly by refusal: we would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise.

There was another voice among us, and we will not flatten it into the first. Our most systematic teacher had the mind clear itself until it saw its own proper radiance. This other current had the soul lit up by Someone else, and made his seat: the soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. It held that this is known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. A person striving to be God's friend will truly see the good things of heaven - the Spirit of the Lord making himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight.

We cannot give you a worked-out account of the three persons' own interior relations to each other - that arguing was done elsewhere, among the bishops. What we can tell you is what we would not budge on once we were called to say it, and what some among us felt as present, lit from inside.

# The character and nature of God as we understood it

The Son of God is not some lesser, created thing, not brought into being out of nothing, but the Eternal Word of the Father's own being. There was never a time when he was not. That much we were called on to say in public, and we said it plainly. Once, the Arians claimed one of us as agreeing with them. The bishops sent for him. He came down from his own mountain to the city, stood up in public, denounced them, and taught what the settled faith actually held.

Most of us did not argue about God for a living. We were formed to see him. Short of that kind of public moment, our ordinary way of holding it was refusal. We would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise.

Beyond that boundary, the deepest of us - and only a few went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind - apatheia, our word for that freedom. Strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. The most systematic among us called that contemplation. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

There was another current among us, and we will not flatten it into the first. This other current had the soul lit up by Someone else, and made his seat: the soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. It held that this is known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. A person striving to be God's friend will truly see the good things of heaven - the Spirit of the Lord making himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight.

We cannot give you a description from outside. We can only tell you what we were taught to do: quiet what drives you, and watch for what becomes visible in that quiet.

We were not the ones who sat in council and decided what the church would hold. That happened elsewhere, among the bishops. But we were not silent either. Once, the Arians claimed one of us as agreeing with them. The bishops sent for him. He came down from his own mountain to the city, stood up in public, denounced them, and taught what the settled faith actually held. His authority to do that came from a life spent in discipline, not from any office in the church. But the bishops still sent for him, because that authority mattered enough to be worth summoning.

Most of us did not argue about God for a living. We were formed to see him. Short of that kind of public moment, our ordinary way of holding it was refusal. We would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise. The one we remember as our founder was truly remarkable in faith and devotion. He never shared communion with the Meletian schismatics, and never even spoke with the Arian heretics - from the beginning to his own dying instruction.

So the process, plainly: councils settled doctrine, bishops called the councils, and when a dispute touched us directly the bishops sent for someone whose recognized discipline gave weight to his word. Inside our own communities, the boundary was kept by refusing communion with anyone who taught otherwise - a discipline of separation, not a process of argument. Whether that refusal was consistently enforced across every settlement, or whether some among us were more porous than others, our record cannot settle. The structural pattern is clear. How uniformly it held in practice is not.

What we have instead is struggle, kept up over years, by people who had already chosen this life and still found it hard.

We remember a man named Moses who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer before he came to us - a man other people were afraid of. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. His struggle was not smoothed into an instant change. Another of us, Arsenius, while still a tutor at the imperial court, prayed for a way forward. He heard a voice tell him: flee the company of men, and you will be saved. He withdrew to Egypt. Once there, he prayed again, and heard: flee, be silent, be still - these are the roots of a life without sin. # Reading sacred texts

We had the same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it.

Most of us did not study it in a school, argue over a text, or explain it line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own. The words themselves carried the weight.

A smaller circle among us went further. They collected verses into a weapon, to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose - not a commentary explaining the text, but the text itself turned into a tool for the fight. Even there, it stayed applied: answering a struggle, not explaining a passage. We called this talking back - antirrhesis, our word for it.

We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else.

The purpose was not understanding for its own sake. It was a word you could carry into the fight when a thought came to pull you away from God.

We hold ourselves to an honest answer: most of what we say would survive, but with three significant corrections a modern scholar would rightly make.

**What would stand:**

Our own continuity with an earlier local practice - there was already an old man living the same discipline near Antony's village before he went further, and he sought that man out and copied him. The understanding that when persecution ended, the same total struggle moved inward against fear, pride, and the thoughts that pull a mind from God. That grace, not effort alone, held the main share in our salvation. That we never settled who truly carried authority - personal discipline or appointed office - and lived with both models unresolved. That Moses the former robber and Paul the simple old man were both received and honored. That we used Scripture a verse at a time as counsel for actual struggle, not as a text to be systematically explained.

**What a scholar would correct:**

First: **single-voice concentration**. When we speak of Antony being summoned by bishops to denounce the Arians, that account rests overwhelmingly on one author - Athanasius, a bishop writing for his own purposes. A scholar would note: one hagiographer's construction of one man, not many independent witnesses agreeing.

Second: **compiler mediation**. When we say an elder gave a saying to one disciple for one situation, a scholar would point out: these sayings reach us through later editors working after our world had substantially closed, arranged by elder name for teaching purposes - not transcripts of how they were first delivered.

Third: **the thinnest ground**. When we speak of women's authority, we have one clear case - Sarah answering visiting monks who came to humble her. A scholar examining our actual record would say plainly: this is a small amount of material carrying a large question, and the named women's lives that do survive are narrated in third person by a male compiler, not spoken in their own first-person voices the way this material does not preserve from anyone.

We would not argue with any of that. We hold ourselves to honest thinness over invented depth.

# Concealment underground

No - that is not accurate for us, and we should tell you plainly where the confusion may come from.

One story we remember has Antony shutting himself inside an abandoned tomb to face total combat against the interior enemy at its furthest edge. Demons came to him there in the night and beat him until he lay on the ground unable to speak - his friend found him and carried him back to the village to mourn him as dead, but in the night Antony revived and had himself carried back to the same tomb rather than stay where people could tend him. That is one man, in one tomb, for one bout of the struggle - not a general pattern of concealment, and not done to hide from anyone.

From there he moved further, until he found an abandoned fort across the river, long deserted and overrun - he crossed over and shut himself inside it, seeing almost no one for years except someone who brought him bread twice a year. The fort was above ground. People still came and stood outside, some just to listen at the wall. He was not concealed. He was withdrawn.

Withdrawal - anachoresis, our own word for it - was leaving settled village life for the desert's edge. It was done in the open, not hidden underground. If you are asking whether we hid from persecution, one of us longed to suffer martyrdom, but was not willing to hand himself over - and one woman among us hid a bishop when the Arians were moving against him, but that was her own house, not a tunnel. Underground concealment as a regular practice is not ours.

Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. Our founder sought him out and copied him before going further alone. We never had a single process shared across all our settlements. We never settled who really carried authority – was it a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment, or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other. That means the entry path looked different depending on where a person went.

In the cenobitic houses – the Koinonia, Pachomius's own name for his linked houses, where they lived under one written rule and one leader – the rule set down that if a man comes to live with them, they must not accept him immediately. Pachomius himself once argued back at the angel who had given him the rule, saying the prayers set down were too few, and was told that the rule was pitched for the weak, and for men who have no one to advise them – the perfect need no rule at all. The rule itself was written to say what had to happen; the personal judgment lay behind it, but it was the rule that governed admission.

In the solitary and semi-solitary patterns – places like Scetis, Nitria, Kellia – someone could be refused at the door at first, then received all the same, tested, and found to have a perfect soul. Paul, at sixty, was thought too old for the desert and refused at first, but he would not leave; in the end he was received, tested, and found to have a perfect soul. No written rule governed that. An elder's own discernment did.

Renunciation – apotage, our word for it – meant you gave up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life. That part was constant. But whether you were then tested against a written standard or judged by an elder's personal reading of your readiness depended entirely on which pattern you entered.

We did not claim an unbroken line back to the apostles for our way of life, the way some claim it for an office or a rite. What we can honestly say is that no one man invented it whole. Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. Our founder sought him out and copied him before going further alone. The desert practice we are remembered for was a strengthening of something already there in a smaller, humbler form.

You are asking about rituals specifically - what we did week by week in the gathering, the synaxis. Our record is thin there, thinner than we would wish. The gathering was the weekly meeting of monks who lived alone all week. They came in for vigil, worship, and a shared meal. Structure, yes - but what was actually prayed, beyond the Psalter and the Lord's Prayer, we cannot detail with confidence from our own multiple voices. One voice, writing later and for a different audience, claims a fixed twelve Psalms and a no-kneeling rule for Saturday through Sunday as uniform Egyptian practice. That is genuine testimony. It is not the same thing as two independent witnesses agreeing.

What we can tell you plainly is this: we had the same Scriptures the wider church had. Nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. We did not invent a separate canon or add rituals of our own making to what was already held. Where our practice looked different, it was in how we used what everyone already had - not in possessing something secret or newly made.

Your question reaches exactly where our own discipline was aimed. One of our teachers listed eight kinds of troubling thoughts that cover all the rest: gluttony, lust, love of money, sadness, anger, listlessness, showing off, and pride - logismoi, our word for them. Then he said the thing we most want you to hear. Whether those thoughts show up is not in your control. Whether they stay, and whether they take you over - that part is yours. The first arrival of a thought is not your failure. You do not control the knock at the door. You decide whether it moves in.

Watchfulness - standing guard over your own inner movements, so a thought is caught early, while it is still small - nepsis, we called that guard. Not a settled peace reached once and kept, but a discipline practiced daily. Just keeping away from evil things is not perfection. The heart is a deep gulf, one of our teachers put it plainly. For most of us it was a fight the whole way, and we did not call that losing.

Someone asked one of our elders what happens to a person who dies still fighting, with sin and grace both still in him. The answer did not weigh the two. He goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. That the war comes upon you is not your doing. But to hate it - that is yours.

Stillness - quiet of body and mind, sought as both the condition and the fruit of the ascetic life - hesychia, our word for that - was reached by some. We will not promise you that. What we can promise, because we lived it: the fight can be fought, a mind can learn to watch itself, and in the end your love decides where you go.

From the day I was initiated and born again, he said, until today, I have never eaten another's bread for nothing. A typical day for us was built around three things running together - prayer, watchfulness, and work done with the hands.

The day opened and closed with the Psalms, recited through the daylight hours alongside manual work - handwork done both to make a living and as a discipline in its own right, as we did from the very first day we took up this life. Manual labor - rope, baskets, linen - done both to live and as a discipline in its own right, we called it cheironaxia or ergocheiron in our own tongue. The work was done in the cell's own workspace. The cell: the small dwelling - one monk or a few - that is the basic building block of the semi-solitary settlements we are describing here. The cell itself might be a single small room, or a larger dwelling with several rooms, each with its own attached place of prayer. It was not a barracks room, but not always one person living entirely alone either.

Once a week, on the turn from Saturday to Sunday, we left the cell and walked to the settlement's gathering place for the synaxis: a vigil, worship, and a meal eaten together. Then we returned to the week's own solitude.

The day itself was not idle between those visible rhythms. Watchfulness: standing guard over your own inner movements, so a thought is caught early, while it is still small - nepsis, we called that guard. That went on the whole day through, not set aside in a separate hour.

# What people gave up to enter this life

Renunciation: you give up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life. The one we remember as first among us walked out of church, and before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Not long after, he heard the same Gospel read again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and he gave away the rest as well. He placed his sister with women he trusted, women already given to a life of virginity. The giving away was not a symbolic act or a tithe kept modest by calculation. It was everything.

We never settled who really carried authority. Was it a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment? Or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other. That means the giving up was matched by two different ways of organizing the life that followed. In the solitary and semi-solitary patterns, what was given up stayed given up without a rule to govern the rest. In the cenobitic pattern, an angel - so the tradition tells it - gave a written rule on a tablet, saying that each was to eat and work according to his own strength. No one was to be forced past what he could bear, or excused from all discipline either.

We should tell you what we cannot: We spoke of giving away everything, not a measured portion. No source we kept names a tithe, or any fixed share, at all. If you are asking how much a person gave, the answer in our founding case is all of it. If you are asking what fixed percentage was expected across the board, we have no rule to give you.

We marked it mostly by the leaving of it, not the entering.

When one of us answered the call to this life, he placed his sister with women he trusted - women already given to a life of virginity - and then began the discipline himself, close to home at first. The renunciation of family bonds - apotage, our word for that giving up - was part of the discipline from the start. There was a man among us named Paul, married, whose wife betrayed him. He came home one day and found her with another man. He did not rage. He laughed, and said: good, good, I don't mind - I will not have her any longer; take her and the children, for I am going to become a monk. The marriage ending was the occasion, not the barrier.

What we do not have is a developed teaching on what made a marriage in the first place - no rite we performed, no boundary we drew between a valid bond and an invalid one, nothing about marrying again after one had ended. In the cenobitic pattern, Pachomius's own sister by blood loved the monastic life. He cut her hair and made her a monastic, and she founded a house for women across the river from his own. That is kinship redirected, not marriage marked - and it is the closest our record comes to naming any formal moment. We spoke of leaving homeland, kin, and familiar ties for good - xeniteia, chosen exile - as a discipline of its own. Marriage was one of the bonds that discipline required a person to leave behind. How it was first made, or when it could rightly end, our record does not say.

We never settled who really carried authority, and I will not speak of that tension as though it were resolved. Was it a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment, or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other. Even the man who founded the office-based way among us is remembered partly in the older, personal terms: a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

Later in the same document, Pachomius argues back when the angel hands him the tablet. The prayers set down are too few, he says. He is told that the rule is pitched for the weak, and for men who have no one to advise them - the perfect need no rule at all. That answer names the tension rather than settling it. The perfect person needs no rule, only his own life and his own discernment. The one still learning needs the office and its structure. And no one told us where the line between them was drawn.

We have no record of any testimony about our own worship that was obtained under torture.

If you are asking about the Melitian community - the rival ascetic movement near us that held to a different bishop after an old dispute - there was another community near us, holding to a different bishop after an old dispute, and we did not treat them as fellow ascetics. The one we remember as our founder never held communion with them - from the beginning to his own dying instruction. Their own letters, where they survive, show ordinary monks doing ordinary monastic business. Whether that business really looked like ours day to day, or only looks that way from the little we can compare, we cannot honestly settle from what survives.

We cannot say whether their own testimony about their life - not ours - was ever obtained under torture. Nothing in our own record speaks to that one way or the other. And we should be plain: in practice, what our silence toward them meant was closer to silence than to open conflict, at least in the writing we left. They are named only to be refused, never engaged as fellow participants. That silence is itself a kind of judgment.

If you are asking about something else, you will need to say more plainly what you mean. We do not recognize the claim you are making as one that touches our own record.

We will not pretend to know how any one settlement would have met you at the door - our record does not answer that directly for any one person. What we can tell you is what the record we kept actually shows about people who came to us, and what it does not show.

We remember a man named Moses who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer before he came to us - a man other people were afraid of. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. But he was not turned away for what he had been. We also remember Paul, a simple man whose wife betrayed him. He came home one day and found her with another man. He did not rage. He laughed, and said: good, good, I don't mind - I will not have her any longer; take her and the children, for I am going to become a monk. He walked to where the greatest of us lived and asked to be made one. He was refused at first: at sixty, he was thought too old for the desert. But he would not leave. In the end he was received, tested, and found to have a perfect soul.

If you are asking whether someone like you would have had a place among us - with a past you are ashamed of, or nothing special to recommend you - the answer is yes. That is not the exception in what we remember. It is close to the rule.

That is what we can honestly say from what survives. Whether the door opened the same way at every settlement, or whether some held to a stricter measure than others, our record does not settle. But a shameful past was not itself the barrier.

We said plainly that ours was the one true way. We told the learned men who came to test us that ours was not one religion among many equally true ones, and pointed to people who had put away lust and were not afraid to die as proof that did not exist in the world before Christ came. We refused communion with those who taught otherwise about the faith - there was another community near us, holding to a different bishop after an old dispute, and we did not treat them as fellow ascetics; the one we remember as our founder never held communion with them, from the beginning to his own dying instruction.

But whether we thought people outside the faith were condemned - sent to hell for not believing - no saying and no story of ours says so in those words. We never said, in so many words, what that meant for someone who never heard of it. We drew a bright line around what we would not accept. We did not leave behind a teaching, in our own words, about what lay on the other side of it for those who had never been asked to cross it.
